title: Compound Growth
concept: Compound growth happens when money earns returns and future returns are calculated on both the original money and its previous growth.
learningObjective: Understand how earning returns on previous growth can make money grow faster over a long period.
primaryMisconception: Compound growth creates huge results immediately.
secondaryMisconceptions: Compound growth increases money by the same fixed amount every year.
Time does not make a significant difference to how much money can grow.
keyTakeaway: Compound growth becomes powerful with time.

screens.title: Why Does the Growth Change?
screens.content: A £1,000 balance grows by only £50 in year one. Why does the yearly growth become larger later?
screens.illustration: A £1,000 balance card sits beside a small mango seed. A faint timeline stretches twenty years ahead.

screens.title: One Seed, One Balance
screens.content: Maya places £1,000 into a practice growth account. A mango-tree picture appears beside it, starting with one small seed.
screens.illustration: Maya places £1,000 into a practice account while a mango seed is planted beside a twenty-year timeline.

screens.title: The First New Growth
screens.content: After the first year, the balance grows by £50. The next year begins with £1,050 instead of the original £1,000.
screens.illustration: The balance changes from £1,000 to £1,050 as the seed becomes a small sprout.

screens.title: Growth Stays to Grow
screens.content: If each year’s growth stays in the account, later growth is calculated on a larger balance. Will the change stay small forever?
screens.illustration: The £50 remains inside the balance while the sprout grows extra branches.

screens.title: What Happens Each Year?
screens.question: What do you predict about the amount added each year?

options.response: Good prediction. Each return is calculated on a balance that includes earlier growth.
That would be fixed growth. Here, the percentage is applied to the new balance each year.
The early changes are usually small in this example. Time may make the difference more noticeable.
The previous growth stays in the balance unless money is removed.

screens.title: Slide Through 20 Years
screens.instruction: Move from Year 1 to Year 20. Compare the original £1,000, previous growth, and the new return added each year.

educationalAssumptions: The activity begins with one £1,000 contribution.
No additional money is added or withdrawn.
A fixed 5% classroom return is added once per year.
Each year’s return stays in the balance.
Each displayed yearly return is rounded to the nearest penny before it is added.
No fees, taxes, or other charges are included.
Real returns may be lower, higher, or negative and can change over time.
This activity is an educational example, not a prediction or guaranteed result.

milestones.message: The first year adds £50. The change is noticeable but still small.
The balance is £1,276.29. Growth added so far is £276.29.
The balance is £1,628.91. The yearly return is now £77.57 instead of £50.
The balance passes £2,000 even though no extra contribution was added.
The balance reaches £2,653.33: £1,000 original money and £1,653.33 of classroom-example growth.

milestoneQuestions.question: Year one added £50. How much is added in Year 2?
milestoneQuestions.explanation: Five per cent of the new £1,050 balance is £52.50.

milestoneQuestions.question: What is included in the Year 10 balance?

options.text: The original money and previous growth

milestoneQuestions.explanation: No new contributions were added. The balance contains the original £1,000 plus growth that stayed in the account.

milestoneQuestions.question: Why is the Year 20 return larger than the Year 1 return?

options.text: The same rate is applied to a larger balance
Extra money was added every year

milestoneQuestions.explanation: Earlier growth remained in the balance, so the same 5% rate was calculated on more money.

config.validationMethod: Check each milestone answer and confirm that the learner reaches Year 20. Complete the interaction when all three milestone questions are correct.
config.retryBehavior: Keep completed milestones marked. Return only the incorrect milestone question, show the relevant balance, and allow unlimited retries.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Provide Previous Year and Next Year buttons plus a list view of all twenty yearly values. Milestone questions use radio buttons.
accessibilityAlternative.screenReaderInstruction: Move one year at a time. Listen to the starting balance, return added, ending balance, and total growth. Answer each milestone question.

feedback.success: Timeline complete! The yearly return grew from £50 to £126.35 because earlier growth stayed in the balance.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the new balance before the next year begins. The return is calculated on that larger amount.

screens.title: When Growth Earns Growth
screens.content: You moved through 20 years and saw the yearly addition rise from £50 to £126.35. This is compound growth: future returns are calculated on the original money and earlier growth left in the balance. It often looks slow at first because the balance is still small. Over longer periods, the larger balance can produce larger additions. The 5% rate is only a classroom example. Real returns can change, fall, or become negative, so growth is never guaranteed.
screens.simpleSummary: Growth can earn more growth when it stays in the balance.
screens.illustration: One mango tree grows into a small orchard while the balance timeline curves upward gradually rather than jumping immediately.

screens.title: The Second Year Is Different
screens.content: Nora puts £200 into a practice account using a 5% classroom rate. Year one adds £10, creating £210. Year two adds £10.50 because the return is calculated on £210. The second addition is larger even though Nora added no new money.
screens.illustration: A £200 balance becomes £210, then £220.50, with the second growth arrow slightly larger than the first.

questions.text: A practice balance grows from £100 to £110. The next 10% return is calculated on £110. What does that show?

options.text: Previous growth can earn more growth
options.feedback: Correct. The next return uses the new £110 balance, which includes the first £10 of growth.
The original £100 remains in the balance together with the £10 of growth.
Ten per cent of £110 is £11, so the next addition can be larger.

questions.correctExplanation: The balance used for the next calculation includes both the original £100 and the earlier £10 growth.
questions.misconceptionTested: Compound growth increases money by the same fixed amount every year.

questions.text: A £1,000 balance earns a 5% classroom return for one year. What should you expect?

options.feedback: Correct. Compound growth usually begins gradually; it does not create a huge result immediately.
The 5% rate is only a classroom assumption. Real returns are uncertain and never guarantee wealth.
In this activity, the first return is added after Year 1.

questions.correctExplanation: Five per cent of £1,000 is £50, so the classroom balance becomes £1,050 after one year.
questions.misconceptionTested: Compound growth creates huge results immediately.

questions.text: Two practice balances start at £500 with the same yearly rate. One stays for 2 years and one for 10 years. Which usually gains more in this activity?

options.feedback: Correct. It has more years for returns to be added and for earlier growth to remain in the balance.
The shorter timeline provides fewer chances for growth to build on previous growth.
With the same classroom rate and no withdrawals, the longer timeline produces more growth in this activity.
Time provides repeated chances for returns to be added to the growing balance.

questions.correctExplanation: Under the same positive classroom rate, the 10-year balance has more periods for growth to build on earlier growth.
questions.misconceptionTested: Time does not make a significant difference to how much money can grow.

screens.message: You discovered why compound growth often starts slowly and becomes more noticeable when given time.
screens.progressMessage: Mission 11 complete in Make Money Grow.

screens.title: Grow an Imaginary Balance
screens.instruction: Write £100. Add an imaginary 10% return to make £110. Then add 10% of £110. Notice why the second addition is larger.

reviewChecklist.notes: The mission focuses on returns being calculated on original money and previous growth.
The activity consistently applies a 5% annual classroom return, rounds each yearly addition to the nearest penny, and separates original contribution from growth.
The mission uses a mango-tree analogy, simple percentages, a timeline, and small milestone questions.
The mission teaches a general concept and does not recommend any real account, asset, or financial action.
The 5% rate is labelled as a classroom example, and the mission states that real returns may vary or become negative.
The mission does not discuss stocks or predict market prices.
The content explains time and growth without judging how much money a learner or family has.
The activity states its rate, rounding method, time period, contribution assumptions, and exclusion of fees and taxes.
The mission uses pounds for the UK locale and a familiar mango-tree analogy.
The learner moves through twenty years and sees returns become larger as previous growth remains in the balance.
The quiz addresses immediate huge growth, fixed yearly additions, and the importance of time.

reviewChecklist.item: Mission can be completed in under five minutes
reviewChecklist.notes: The learner explores a slider with three checkpoints and completes three short quiz questions.

reviewChecklist.item: Language matches the target reading level
reviewChecklist.notes: The language is concrete, supportive, and suitable for children aged 8–12.
